﴿By the winds that scatter (dust) with dispersal, and those that carry a load, and those that glide with ease, and those that distribute by command.﴾ ﴿What you are promised is surely true, and the Judgment will surely come to pass.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By the winds that scatter (dust) with dispersal.﴾ Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Abdullah ibn Najiyah narrated to us, Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Makki ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, al-Ju'ayd ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Khusayfah, from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, that a man said to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I passed by a man who was asking about the difficult interpretation of the Qur'an." Umar said: "O Allah, enable me to deal with him." The man came to Umar one day while he was wearing garments and a turban, and Umar was reciting the Qur'an. When Umar finished, the man stood before him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is (﴿By the winds that scatter (dust) with dispersal﴾)?" Umar stood up, bared his forearms, and began to beat him. Then he said: "Dress him in his clothes, put him on a saddle-less mount, and take him to his tribe. Then let him stand up as a preacher and say: 'Indeed Sabigh [[Sabigh, on the pattern of Amir, the son of Asal, with a kasra on the ayn. He used to trouble people with obscure matters and questions about the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an. Umar banished him to Basra after beating him, wrote to its governor not to shelter him, and forbade people from sitting with him (al-Taj).]] sought knowledge and erred in it.'" He remained despised among his people after having been a leader among them.

It is also narrated from Amir ibn Wathilah that Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is (﴿By the winds that scatter (dust) with dispersal﴾)?" He said: "Woe to you! Ask in order to understand, and do not ask in order to trouble (others)." (﴿By the winds that scatter (dust) with dispersal﴾) means the winds; (﴿those that carry a load﴾) means the clouds; (﴿those that glide with ease﴾) means the ships; (﴿those that distribute by command﴾) means the angels.

al-Harith narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that (﴿By the winds that scatter (dust) with dispersal﴾) he said: the winds. (﴿Those that carry a load﴾) he said: the clouds, which carry water just as four-legged animals carry a load. (﴿Those that glide with ease﴾) he said: the ships laden (with cargo). (﴿Those that distribute by command﴾) he said: the angels who bring various commands: Jibril with severity, Mika'il, who is the bearer of mercy, and the Angel of Death, who brings death.

al-Farra' said: It has been said that they bring various commands concerning abundance and scarcity, rain and death, and events. It is said: the wind scatters the dust, (taruhu) dharwan, and (tadhriyhi) dharyan.

Then it has been said: (﴿By the winds that scatter (dust)﴾) and what follows it are oaths, and when the Lord swears by something, He thereby establishes its honour. It has also been said that the meaning is "By the Lord of the winds that scatter (dust)." The answer (to the oath) is (﴿What you are promised is surely true﴾), that is, what you are promised of good and evil, reward and punishment, is (﴿surely true﴾), with no falsehood in it. The meaning of (﴿surely true﴾) is "truthful," and the noun has taken the place of the verbal noun.

(﴿And the Judgment will surely come to pass﴾) means that the recompense will descend upon you. Then He began another oath, saying: (﴿By the heaven with its paths. Indeed you are in a contradictory saying﴾).

It has also been said that (﴿those that scatter﴾) refers to women who give birth, because in their wombs there is the scattering of creation, for they scatter the children, and so they are called (﴿dhariyat﴾). He swore by them because of what is in their wombs of the righteous servants of Allah. He singled out women for this, rather than men, although each of them scatters. This is for two reasons. First, because they are containers in which men do not share, so the two kinds of scattering are gathered in them, and hence they were singled out for mention. Second, the scattering in them lasts longer, and they are closer in time to physical contact.

(﴿Those that carry a load﴾) means the clouds. It has also been said that it refers to women when they become heavy with pregnancy. The word (al-wiqr), with a kasra on the waw, is the weight of a load on a back or in a belly. It is said: "He came carrying his load (wiqrahu), and he has loaded his camel (awqara ba'iranahu)." The word (al-wiqr) is most often used for the load of a mule or a donkey, while (al-wasq) is used for the load of a camel. It is said: "This woman is (muwqarah), with a fatha on the qaf, if she has carried a heavy burden." It is also said that "the palm tree became laden (awqarat al-nakhlah)" when its fruit became abundant, and it is said: "a palm that is (muqirah), (muqirun), or (muqarah)," and (muqar) has been reported, which is irregular, because the verb belongs to the palm tree. The form (muqir), with a kasra on the qaf, was used according to the pattern of your saying "a pregnant woman (imra'ah hamil)," because the bearing of a tree is compared to the bearing of women. As for (muqar), with a fatha, it is anomalous. It has been reported in the verse of Labid describing palm trees:

*Clustered (palms) standing in a fertile valley, / they bore fruit, and some of them are laden and covered.*

The plural is (mawaqir). As for (al-waqr), with a fatha, it means heaviness of the ear, and his ear became (tauqar), meaning he became deaf. The regular form of its verbal noun would be with a vowel on the middle radical, but it came with a sukun, and this has already been discussed in (al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 404.]]).

(﴿Those that glide with ease﴾) means the ships that run with the winds with ease to wherever they are directed. It has also been said that it refers to the clouds. On this view, there are two interpretations of their gliding with ease: first, to wherever Allah directs them among the lands and regions; second, it means the ease of their movement, which is well known among the Arabs, as al-A'sha said:

*Her gait, from the house of her neighbour, / is like the walk of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty.*

*Her gait, from the house of her neighbour, / is like the walk of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty.*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 51, verses 7–14:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky full of paths﴾. It has been said: what is meant by "the sky" here is the clouds that shade the earth. It has also been said: it is the raised sky. Ibn Umar said: it is the seventh heaven. This was related by al-Mahdawi, al-Tha'labi, al-Mawardi and others.

Regarding (al-Hubuk), there are seven views:

The first: Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: it means "possessing good, even creation." Ikrimah also said this, and he said: "Have you not seen the weaver, when he weaves a cloth and perfects its weaving?" From this one says *habaka al-thawba yahbiku-hu habkan*, meaning he perfected its weaving. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Everything you make firm and do well, you have *ihtabaktahu*."

The second: it means "possessing adornment." This was said by al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. From al-Hasan also: "possessing stars," and this is the third view.

The fourth: al-Dahhak said: "possessing paths." It is said of what you see in water and sand when the wind strikes it: *hubuk*. Similar is the statement of al-Farra', who said: "*al-hubuk* is the breaking up of anything, like sand when still wind passes over it, and like water standing when wind passes over it. A coat of iron mail has *hubuk*, and a curly hair has its breaks, *hubuk*." In the hadith about the Dajjal it is said that his hair is *hubuk*. Zuhayr said:

*Crowned with the roots of the najm plant, woven by a violent wind upon the sunlit part of its water, are its ripples.* [[The *najm* is every plant that has no stalk and grows around water, like the *akalil*. *Rih kharik* means a strong wind. *Li-dahima'ihi* means what is exposed to the sun of the water, i.e. what appears. The verse describes a pool.]]

But they are far from the servants, so they do not see them.

The fifth: *dhat al-shiddah* (possessing strength). This was said by Ibn Zayd, who recited: ﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens]﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 3 (169)]]. *Al-mahbuk* means one of strong build, of a horse or other animal. Imru' al-Qays said:

*He has set out, carrying me on his nose, with his flanks all in one piece, strongly knit and firm.* [[*Al-atl* means the entire flank. It is also said to mean other things.]]

Another said:

*When the religion became disordered, I prepared for it a horse, high-withered, well-knit at the shoulder-blade.* [[The verse is by Abu Dawud describing a horse. *Al-katad*, with the *ta'* either fatha or kasra, is the joining place of the two shoulders in a human or a horse.]]

In a hadith, 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) used to *tahtabik* beneath the shift during prayer, meaning she tightened and secured her waist-wrap.

The sixth: *dhat al-safaqah* (possessing thickness). This was said by Khusayf. From it comes "a thick cloth" and "a thick-faced person," meaning clearly thick.

The seventh: the meaning of the *turuq* is the Milky Way in the sky, named so because it is like the trace of a weaver's comb (*al-majarr*). (*Al-hubuk*) is the plural of *hibak*. The rajiz said:

*As if the weaver had covered it with a carpet, in whose embroidery are *hibak* lines.*

*Al-hibak* and *al-habikah* mean a path in sand or the like. The plural of *al-hibak* is *hubuk*, and the plural of *al-habikah* is *haba'ik*. *Al-habakah* is like *al-'abakah*, which is a grain of sawiq (roasted flour), according to al-Jawhari.

It is related from al-Hasan regarding his statement (*dhat al-hubuk*): (*al-hubki*), (*al-habki*), (*al-hubki*), (*al-hubki*) and (*al-habki*), and [he also recited (*al-hubuki*)] like the group. It is related from Ikrimah and Abu Mijlaz: (*al-hubuki*). (*Al-hubuk*)'s singular is *habikah*, and (*al-habk*) is its lightened form. (*Al-hibak*)'s singular is *hibkah*. Whoever reads (*al-hubaki*), its singular is *hubkah*, like *burqah* and *buraq*, or *hubukah*, like *zulmah* and *zulam*. Whoever reads (*al-hibiki*) it is like *ibil* and *ibl*, and (*al-habk*) is a lightened form of it. [[*Al-atl* means the entire flank. It is also said to mean other things.]]

Whoever reads (*al-hibuki*) it is an anomaly (*shadhdh*), since there is no *fi'ul* pattern in Arabic speech. It is taken as a mixing of dialects, as if he broke the *ha'* so as to break the *ba'*, then imagined (*al-hubuki*) and so pronounced the *ba'* with a *damma*. Al-Mahdawi said all of this.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. This is the answer to the oath whose subject is (*wa-al-sama'*), meaning: indeed you, O people of Makkah, are in a discordant saying about Muhammad and the Qur'an, some affirming and some denying. It has been said: it was revealed about the *muqtasimun* (those who divided the Qur'an). It has also been said: their discord is their saying "he is a sorcerer," "rather a poet," "rather he invented it," "rather he is mad," "rather he is a soothsayer," "rather it is the fables of the ancients." It has also been said: their discord is that some of them denied the resurrection and some doubted it. It has also been said: what is meant is the worshippers of idols and images, who acknowledge that Allah is their Creator and yet worship others.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾. That is, whoever is diverted from belief in Muhammad and the Qur'an is diverted, according to al-Hasan and others. It has been said: the meaning is that whoever wants to believe is diverted from belief by their saying: "it is sorcery, and soothsaying, and fables of the ancients." It has been said: the meaning is that whoever Allah protects is turned away from that discord. *Afakahu yafikuhu afkan* means he turned him around and diverted him from something. From this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 205]]. Mujahid said: the meaning of (*yu'fakun 'anhu man ufik*) is (*yu'fan 'anhu man ufin*), and *al-afn* is corruption of the intellect. Al-Zamakhshari: it is also read (*yu'fan 'anhu man ufin*), meaning whoever is deprived is deprived of it, from *afina al-darʻ* when he exhausted its milk by milking. Qutrub said: "he is deceived who is deceived." Al-Yazidi said: "he is repelled who is repelled." The meaning is one, and all of it returns to the meaning of diversion.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Killed are the fabricators﴾. In the exegesis: "cursed are the liars." Ibn Abbas said: that is, "killed are the doubters," meaning the soothsayers. al-Hasan said: they are those who say, "We shall not be raised." The meaning of (*qutila*) is that these are among those for whom it is due that they be prayed against to be killed at the hands of the believers. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of (*qutila*) is "cursed." He said: and (*al-kharrasun*) are the liars who speculate about what they do not know, saying: "Muhammad is mad, a liar, a sorcerer, a poet." This is a supplication against them, because whoever Allah curses is in the position of one who is killed and destroyed. Ibn al-Anbari said: He taught us to pray against them, meaning: say, "Killed are the fabricators." It is the plural of *kharis*, and *al-khars* is lying, and *al-kharras* is a liar. It is said: *kharasa*, *yakhrusu*, *khurs*, meaning he lied; it is said: *kharasa* and *ikhtarasa*, *khalaqa* and *iktalaqa*, *bashaka* and *ibtashaka*, *siraja* and *istaraja*, and *mana*, with the meaning of lied, as Ibn al-Nahhas related. *Al-khars* also means estimating what is on the palm of ripe dates as dried dates. One says: "the palm was estimated" (*kharasat al-nakhlu*), and the noun is *al-khirs* with a kasra. One says: "What is the estimate (*khirs*) of your palm?" *Al-kharras* is the one who estimates it, so it is a homonym. The root of *al-khurs* is cutting, as was explained earlier in (*al-An'am*) [[See vol. 7, p. 71]]. From it comes *al-kharis* for a canal, because water is cut off into it. *Al-khurs* is a single bead of an earring when it stands alone, since it is cut off from its siblings. *Al-khurs* is also a stick, because it is cut off from its counterparts by the goodness of its fragrance. *Al-khari* is one who has hunger and cold, because he is cut off by it. One says: *kharisa al-rajul* with a kasra, so he is *khari*, meaning hungry and cold. One does not say *kharasa* for hunger without cold, and one says *kharasa* for cold without hunger. *Al-khurs* with a damma or kasra is a ring of gold or silver, and its plural is *al-khirsan*. The statements of the astrologers, and of everyone who claims conjecture and guessing, enter into *al-kharsh*. Ibn Abbas said: they are the *muqtasimun* who divided the paths of Makkah and divided their speech about the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ), in order to turn people away from belief in him.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Who are in heedless confusion, neglectful﴾. *Al-ghamrah* is what covers and overwhelms a thing. From it comes "a deep river" (*nahr ghamr*), meaning one that overwhelms whoever enters it, and from it come *ghamarat al-mawt* (the agonies of death).

(*Sahun*) means frivolous and heedless of the matter of the Hereafter.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They ask: when is the Day of Recompense?﴾ That is, when is the Day of Reckoning. They say this in mockery and doubt about the Resurrection.

﴿On the Day they will be tried over the Fire﴾. (*Yawm*) is in the accusative by way of an implied predicate, meaning: this is the requital, (*on the Day they will be tried over the Fire*). That is, they will be burned. It is from their saying: *fatantu al-dhahab*, meaning I burned it so that you might test it, and the origin of *fitnah* is testing. It has been said: it is indeclinable, built because it is joined to a non-declinable word, and its position is accusative under the previously mentioned estimate, or nominative as an apposition to (*yawm al-din*). Al-Zajjaj said: one says, "I am pleased with a day you are standing," and "a day you stand," and if you wish, you open it with a fatha, and it is in the nominative position; this is put in the accusative though it is in meaning nominative. Ibn Abbas said: (*yuftanun*) means they are punished. From it is the poet's saying:

*Every person among the servants of Allah is oppressed, in the valley of Makkah, subdued and tormented.*

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Taste your trial﴾. That is, it will be said to them: "Taste your punishment." Said by Ibn Zayd. Mujahid: "your burning." Ibn Abbas: that is, "your denial," meaning your recompense. Al-Farra': that is, "your punishment (*which you used to seek to hasten*)" in this world. He said "*hadha*" and did not say "*hadhihi*," because the *fitnah* here means the punishment.

The sixth: *dhat al-safaqah* (possessing thickness). This was said by Khusayf. From it comes "a thick cloth" and "a thick-faced person," meaning clearly thick.

The seventh: the meaning of the *turuq* is the Milky Way in the sky, named so because it is like the trace of a weaver's comb (*al-majarr*). (*Al-hubuk*) is the plural of *hibak*. The rajiz said:

*As if the weaver had covered it with a carpet, in whose embroidery are *hibak* lines.*

*Al-hibak* and *al-habikah* mean a path in sand or the like. The plural of *al-hibak* is *hubuk*, and the plural of *al-habikah* is *haba'ik*. *Al-habakah* is like *al-'abakah*, which is a grain of sawiq (roasted flour), according to al-Jawhari.

It is related from al-Hasan regarding his statement (*dhat al-hubuk*): (*al-hubki*), (*al-habki*), (*al-hubki*), (*al-hubki*) and (*al-habki*), and [he also recited (*al-hubuki*)] like the group. It is related from Ikrimah and Abu Mijlaz: (*al-hubuki*). (*Al-hubuk*)'s singular is *habikah*, and (*al-habk*) is its lightened form. (*Al-hibak*)'s singular is *hibkah*. Whoever reads (*al-hubaki*), its singular is *hubkah*, like *burqah* and *buraq*, or *hubukah*, like *zulmah* and *zulam*. Whoever reads (*al-hibiki*) it is like *ibil* and *ibl*, and (*al-habk*) is a lightened form of it. [[*Al-atl* means the entire flank. It is also said to mean other things.]]

Whoever reads (*al-hibuki*) it is an anomaly (*shadhdh*), since there is no *fi'ul* pattern in Arabic speech. It is taken as a mixing of dialects, as if he broke the *ha'* so as to break the *ba'*, then imagined (*al-hubuki*) and so pronounced the *ba'* with a *damma*. Al-Mahdawi said all of this.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. This is the answer to the oath whose subject is (*wa-al-sama'*), meaning: indeed you, O people of Makkah, are in a discordant saying about Muhammad and the Qur'an, some affirming and some denying. It has been said: it was revealed about the *muqtasimun* (those who divided the Qur'an). It has also been said: their discord is their saying "he is a sorcerer," "rather a poet," "rather he invented it," "rather he is mad," "rather he is a soothsayer," "rather it is the fables of the ancients." It has also been said: their discord is that some of them denied the resurrection and some doubted it. It has also been said: what is meant is the worshippers of idols and images, who acknowledge that Allah is their Creator and yet worship others.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾. That is, whoever is diverted from belief in Muhammad and the Qur'an is diverted, according to al-Hasan and others. It has been said: the meaning is that whoever wants to believe is diverted from belief by their saying: "it is sorcery, and soothsaying, and fables of the ancients." It has been said: the meaning is that whoever Allah protects is turned away from that discord. *Afakahu yafikuhu afkan* means he turned him around and diverted him from something. From this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 205]]. Mujahid said: the meaning of (*yu'fakun 'anhu man ufik*) is (*yu'fan 'anhu man ufin*), and *al-afn* is corruption of the intellect. Al-Zamakhshari: it is also read (*yu'fan 'anhu man ufin*), meaning whoever is deprived is deprived of it, from *afina al-darʻ* when he exhausted its milk by milking. Qutrub said: "he is deceived who is deceived." Al-Yazidi said: "he is repelled who is repelled." The meaning is one, and all of it returns to the meaning of diversion.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Killed are the fabricators﴾. In the exegesis: "cursed are the liars." Ibn Abbas said: that is, "killed are the doubters," meaning the soothsayers. al-Hasan said: they are those who say, "We shall not be raised." The meaning of (*qutila*) is that these are among those for whom it is due that they be prayed against to be killed at the hands of the believers. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of (*qutila*) is "cursed." He said: and (*al-kharrasun*) are the liars who speculate about what they do not know, saying: "Muhammad is mad, a liar, a sorcerer, a poet." This is a supplication against them, because whoever Allah curses is in the position of one who is killed and destroyed. Ibn al-Anbari said: He taught us to pray against them, meaning: say, "Killed are the fabricators." It is the plural of *kharis*, and *al-khars* is lying, and *al-kharras* is a liar. It is said: *kharasa*, *yakhrusu*, *khurs*, meaning he lied; it is said: *kharasa* and *ikhtarasa*, *khalaqa* and *iktalaqa*, *bashaka* and *ibtashaka*, *siraja* and *istaraja*, and *mana*, with the meaning of lied, as Ibn al-Nahhas related. *Al-khars* also means estimating what is on the palm of ripe dates as dried dates. One says: "the palm was estimated" (*kharasat al-nakhlu*), and the noun is *al-khirs* with a kasra. One says: "What is the estimate (*khirs*) of your palm?" *Al-kharras* is the one who estimates it, so it is a homonym. The root of *al-khurs* is cutting, as was explained earlier in (*al-An'am*) [[See vol. 7, p. 71]]. From it comes *al-kharis* for a canal, because water is cut off into it. *Al-khurs* is a single bead of an earring when it stands alone, since it is cut off from its siblings. *Al-khurs* is also a stick, because it is cut off from its counterparts by the goodness of its fragrance. *Al-khari* is one who has hunger and cold, because he is cut off by it. One says: *kharisa al-rajul* with a kasra, so he is *khari*, meaning hungry and cold. One does not say *kharasa* for hunger without cold, and one says *kharasa* for cold without hunger. *Al-khurs* with a damma or kasra is a ring of gold or silver, and its plural is *al-khirsan*. The statements of the astrologers, and of everyone who claims conjecture and guessing, enter into *al-kharsh*. Ibn Abbas said: they are the *muqtasimun* who divided the paths of Makkah and divided their speech about the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ), in order to turn people away from belief in him.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Who are in heedless confusion, neglectful﴾. *Al-ghamrah* is what covers and overwhelms a thing. From it comes "a deep river" (*nahr ghamr*), meaning one that overwhelms whoever enters it, and from it come *ghamarat al-mawt* (the agonies of death).

(*Sahun*) means frivolous and heedless of the matter of the Hereafter.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They ask: when is the Day of Recompense?﴾ That is, when is the Day of Reckoning. They say this in mockery and doubt about the Resurrection.

﴿On the Day they will be tried over the Fire﴾. (*Yawm*) is in the accusative by way of an implied predicate, meaning: this is the requital, (*on the Day they will be tried over the Fire*). That is, they will be burned. It is from their saying: *fatantu al-dhahab*, meaning I burned it so that you might test it, and the origin of *fitnah* is testing. It has been said: it is indeclinable, built because it is joined to a non-declinable word, and its position is accusative under the previously mentioned estimate, or nominative as an apposition to (*yawm al-din*). Al-Zajjaj said: one says, "I am pleased with a day you are standing," and "a day you stand," and if you wish, you open it with a fatha, and it is in the nominative position; this is put in the accusative though it is in meaning nominative. Ibn Abbas said: (*yuftanun*) means they are punished. From it is the poet's saying:

*Every person among the servants of Allah is oppressed, in the valley of Makkah, subdued and tormented.*

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Taste your trial﴾. That is, it will be said to them: "Taste your punishment." Said by Ibn Zayd. Mujahid: "your burning." Ibn Abbas: that is, "your denial," meaning your recompense. Al-Farra': that is, "your punishment (*which you used to seek to hasten*)" in this world. He said "*hadha*" and did not say "*hadhihi*," because the *fitnah* here means the punishment.

From this one says *habaka al-thawba yahbiku-hu habkan*, meaning he perfected its weaving. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Everything you make firm and do well, you have *ihtabaktahu*."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verse 15–16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be among gardens and springs﴾. When He mentioned the destiny of the disbelievers, He mentioned the destiny of the believers, meaning: they will be in orchards in which there are flowing springs, along the most pleasant of places for enjoyment.

(Ākhidhīna) [taking] is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

(mā ātāhum rabbuhum) meaning: what their Lord gave them of reward and kinds of honours. This is what al-Ḍaḥḥāk said. Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: (ākhidhīna mā ātāhum rabbuhum) meaning: acting upon the obligatory duties (farāʾiḍ).

**Fifth issues: [Five points]** The first point concerns His words, exalted is He: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾. The meaning of *yahja'un* (يَهْجَعُونَ) is "they sleep." *Al-hujū'* (الهُجُوع) is sleep at night, and *al-tahja'* (التَّهْجَاع) is light sleep. Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat said:

*The helmet has pressed upon my head, so I*
*taste no sleep except a light doze.*

And Amr ibn Ma'di Karib, longing for his sister, whom al-Samma, Abu Duraid ibn al-Samma, had taken captive, said:

*Does the one who calls, the one who hears, keep me awake,*
*while my companions are sleeping?*

It is said: *hajaʿa yahjaʿu hujūʿan* and *habagha yahbaghu hubūgh* (with a ghayn), meaning he slept. This was reported by al-Jawhari.

There is disagreement about *mā* (مَا). It is said to be a superfluous complementary particle (ṣila zā'ida), as Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said, and the sense is: "They used to sleep a little of the night and pray most of it." Ata' said: "This applies when they were commanded to perform the night prayer." Abu Dharr [[In z, l, n: (Abu Bakr).]] would tie up his garment and take a staff to lean on, until the concession was revealed: ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 32]]... the verse.

It is also said that *mā* is not a superfluous particle; rather, the pause falls at His words "a little," and then one begins with "of the night they used to sleep not at all," so *mā* is negative, denying that they slept at all. Al-Hasan said: "They did not sleep during the night except a little, and sometimes, when they were energetic, they exerted themselves until dawn."

It is reported from Ya'qub al-Hadrami that he said: "They differed in interpreting this verse. Some of them said: ﴿They used to be few﴾ means their number was small, and then he began: ﴿Of the night, they used to sleep﴾, in the sense of 'of the night they used to sleep.'" Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is corrupt, because the verse indicates only the scarcity of their sleep, not the scarcity of their number. Furthermore, if we began with 'Of the night they used to sleep' in the sense of 'of the night they used to sleep,' there would be no praise of them in this, since all people sleep at night, unless *mā* is a negation."

I say: According to what some people have interpreted, and this is the view of al-Dahhak, that their number was small, the speech is connected to what precedes it, His words: ﴿Indeed, they were before that doers of good﴾, meaning the doers of good were few. Then he resumed: ﴿Of the night they used to sleep﴾. According to the first and second interpretations, ﴿They used to be few of the night﴾ is a new address after the completion of what preceded it, and the pause falls at ﴿they used to sleep﴾. The same applies if you make *qalīlan* (قَلِيلًا) the predicate of *kāna* and take *mā* as the subject, meaning: "They used to be few of the night, their sleeping." So *mā* may be a negation, or it may be a verbal noun with the verb, or it may be in the nominative as a substitute for the subject of *kāna*, the sense being: "Their sleeping used to be little of the night." The accusative of *qalīlan* is, if you consider *mā* a superfluous emphatic particle attached to *yahja'ūn*, on the reading "they were for a little time" or "they used to sleep a little." If you do not consider *mā* superfluous, then *qalīlan* is the predicate of *kāna*, and it is not permissible to put it in the accusative governed by *yahja'ūn*, because if it were governed by *yahja'ūn* with *mā* as a verbal noun, the complement would be placed before the word it complements.

Anas and Qatadah, in interpreting the verse, said: they used to pray between the two evening prayers, the Maghrib and the 'Isha'. Abu al-Aliyah said: they did not sleep between the two evening prayers. Ibn Wahb also said this. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the Ansar, who used to pray the two evening prayers in the mosque of the Prophet ﷺ and then proceed to Quba'. Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn said: they did not sleep until they had prayed the 'Atamah (the late night prayer). Al-Hasan said: "It is as if He regarded their sleep as little in comparison with their wakefulness for prayer." Ibn Abbas and Mutarrif said: there was not a night that passed over them without their praying to Allah during it, either at its beginning or at its middle.

The second point: It is reported from one of the ones who used to perform the night prayer (tahajjud) that a visitor came to him in his dream and recited:

*How can a comforted eye sleep through the night,*
*when it does not know in which of the gatherings it will descend?*

It is reported from a man of the Azd that he said: "I used not to sleep at night, but one night I slept toward the end of the night. Then I saw two youths, the most beautiful I had ever seen, with them were robes. They stood over every worshipper and clothed him in a robe, then they reached the sleepers and did not clothe them. I said to them: 'Clothe me with one of your robes.' They said to me: 'It is not a garment of clothing; it is the good pleasure of Allah, which descends upon every worshipper.'"

It is also reported from Abu Khallad that he said: "A companion of mine told me: 'One night while I was sleeping, the Resurrection was displayed to me. I looked at groups of my brothers whose faces were lit up and whose complexions were radiant, and they were wearing robes above all of creation. I said: What is the matter with these, that they are clothed while people are naked, and their faces are bright while people's faces are dust-covered?' The fourth point: His words, exalted is He: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ are a third praise. Muhammad ibn Sirin and Qatadah said: the *ḥaqq* (حَقّ), "right," here is the obligatory zakat. It is also said that it is a right other than zakat, by which one joins ties of kinship, or hosts a guest, or carries a burden, or enriches the deprived. This was said by Ibn Abbas, because the surah is Meccan, and zakat was made obligatory in Medina. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The strongest view regarding this verse is that it is zakat, due to His words, exalted is He, in Surat (Sa'ala sa'il): ﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right, for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 291]]. The known right is zakat, whose amount, kind and time the Shari'ah has explained. As for other than it, for those who hold such a view, it is not known, because it is neither fixed in amount, nor specified in kind, nor timed."

The fifth point: His words, exalted is He: ﴿For the beggar and the deprived﴾. The *sā'il* (السَّائِل) is the one who asks people because of his poverty. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others.

*Al-maḥrūm* (المَحْرُوم) is the one who has been deprived of wealth. Its identification has been disputed. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others said: the *maḥrūm* is the *muḥārif* (المُحَارَف), who has no share in Islam. 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: the *maḥrūm* is the *muḥārif* whose livelihood is not made easy for him. It is said: "A man *muḥārif* (with a fatha on the ra') means restricted and deprived," which is the opposite of your saying *mubārak* (blessed). It is said: "The livelihood of so-and-so has been *ḥūrif*," when he is made hard-pressed in his subsistence, as if his provision were turned away from him.

Qatadah and al-Zuhri said: the *maḥrūm* is the one who abstains from asking people for anything and whose need is not known. Al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: the *maḥrūm* is the one who comes after the spoils of war and has no share in them. It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ sent a detachment, and they gained and seized spoils. Then a people came after they had finished, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And in their wealth﴾. Ikrimah said: the *maḥrūm* is the one for whom no wealth remains. Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is the one whose fruit, crop or livestock offspring has been struck by disaster. Al-Qurazi said: the *maḥrūm* is the one struck by a calamity (*jā'iḥa*), and then he recited: ﴿Indeed, we are burdened with debt. Rather, we are deprived﴾, a parallel to the story of the people of the garden, where they said: ﴿Rather, we are deprived﴾. Abu Qilabah said: "A man from the people of Yamamah had wealth, then a flood came and took his wealth. A man from among his companions said: 'This is the *maḥrūm*, so give to him.'"

It is also said that he is the one who seeks worldly things while they turn away from him. This is also reported from Ibn Abbas. Abd al-Rahman ibn Humayd said: the *maḥrūm* is the slave. It is said: it is the dog. It is reported that Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz was on the road to Mecca when a dog came, and Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, pulled out the shoulder of a sheep and threw it to him, saying: "They say he is the *maḥrūm*." It is also said: he is the one whose maintenance has become obligatory due to poverty from among the relatives, because he has been deprived of earning for himself, so that his maintenance became obligatory upon the wealth of another. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that he is the one who is deprived of provision. This is a good view, because it encompasses all the other views.

Al-Sha'bi said: "For me today there are seventy years since I reached puberty, asking about the *maḥrūm*, and I am not today more knowledgeable about it than I was then." This was narrated by Shu'bah from Asim al-Ahwal from al-Sha'bi.

Its root in the language is "the one prevented," from *al-ḥirmān* (الحِرْمَان), which is prevention. Alqamah said:

*The one who feeds others on the day of plunder, his own feeding is*
*wherever he turns; and the deprived one is deprived.*

It is reported from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Woe to the rich from the poor on the Day of Resurrection. They will say: 'Our Lord, they wronged us in our rights which were prescribed for us over them.' Then Allah, exalted is He, will say: 'By My might and My majesty, I will bring you near and I will keep them far.'" Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verses 20–23:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who have certainty.﴾ When He mentioned the matter of the two groups, He made clear that on the earth there are signs that point to His power over the resurrection and the raising of the dead. Among them is the regrowth of plants after they have become dry stalks (*hashiman*). Among them is that He ordained within the earth the sustenance that sustains living creatures. Among them is the travel of people through the lands, where they witness the traces of the destruction that fell upon the nations who denied their prophets. Those with certainty (*al-Muqinun*) are the knowers, the verifiers of the oneness of their Lord and of the truthfulness of their Prophet. He singled them out for mention because they are the ones who benefit from those signs and reflect upon them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ It was said: the implied meaning is "and in the earth and in yourselves are signs for those with certainty." Qatadah said: the meaning is that whoever travels through the earth sees signs and lessons, and whoever reflects upon himself knows that he was created to worship Allah. Ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid said: what is meant is the passage of excrement and urine. Al-Sa'ib ibn Sharik said: "He eats and drinks from one place and expels from two places. Had he drunk pure milk, water would have come out of him and also feces; so that is the sign within the self." Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that He created you from dust, and gave you hearing, sight and hearts (*ath-thumma idha antum bashar tantashirun*) [[See vol. 14, p. (17)]]. Al-Suddi said: "And in yourselves" means in your life and your death, and in what enters and leaves you of food. Al-Hasan said: it means in old age after youth, in weakness after strength, and in white hair after black. It was also said: the meaning is in the creation of your selves from a drop of fluid, a clinging clot, a lump of flesh, bone and flesh, until the breathing of the soul; and in the variety of tongues, colours and forms; and other inner and outer signs. It is enough for you to consider the hearts and the intellects placed within them, and the kinds of meanings and arts they have been given; and the tongues, speech, the articulation points of letters, the eyes, the limbs, and all the other body parts, and their ability to perform what they were created for; and the joints arranged in the limbs for bending and flexing; and that when any of them stiffens (*jasa*, meaning the hand's bones stiffen and its flesh diminishes) incapacity comes, and when it goes slack, it drops down. (*Fa-tabaraka Allah ahsan al-khaliqin*) [[See vol. 12, p. (110)]].

(*Afala tubsirun*) means: the sight of the heart, so that they may know the perfection of His power. It was also said: it is the success of the incapable and the deprivation of the prudent. I say: all of that is intended in taking heed. We have already mentioned, in the verse on tawhid in surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 202]], that whatever is in the human body, which is the small world, has a counterpart in the great world, and we mentioned there enough lessons to suffice and satisfy anyone who reflects.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And in heaven is your provision and that which you are promised.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: the provision here is what descends from the sky, of rain and snow, by which the crops grow and creatures live. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: every flowing spring is from snow. It is reported from al-Hasan that whenever he saw clouds he would say to his companions: "By Allah, in it is your provision, but you are deprived of it because of your sins." The scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: "And in heaven is your provision" means "and in the rain is your provision," the rain being called "sky" because it descends from the sky. A poet said [[He is Mu'awwad al-Hukama', Mu'awiyah ibn Malik, and he was called Mu'awwad al-Hukama' because of his saying in this poem:

"I return like them, the wise after me, when the truth has bitten in the vicissitudes of time."]]:

*When the sky falls upon the land of a people,*
*we graze it, even if they are angry.*

Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning is "and upon the Lord of heaven is your provision," and its parallel is: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾. Sufyan al-Thawri said: ﴿And in heaven is your provision﴾ means: with Allah, in the heaven, is your provision. It was also said: the meaning is that in heaven is the decree of your provision, and what is due to you is written in the Mother of the Book (*Umm al-Kitab*). It is reported from Sufyan who said: Wasil al-Ahdab recited ﴿And in heaven is your provision﴾, and said: "Do I not see my provision in the heaven, while I seek it on earth?" So he entered a ruined house and stayed three days without obtaining anything. Then on the third day he found a basket (*dawkhalla*) of fresh dates. He had a brother who had a better intention than him, and he entered with him, and they were two baskets; and that was their practice until Allah separated them by death. (The *dawkhalla*, with the *lam* either doubled or single, is a basket of palm leaves in which dates or fresh dates are placed.) Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid recited ﴿*Raziqukum*﴾ with an alif, and likewise at its end: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider (*ar-Razzaq*)﴾.

﴿And that which you are promised﴾: Mujahid said: that means good and evil. Others said: good specifically. It was also said: evil specifically. It was also said: Paradise, reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah. Al-Dahhak said: ﴿And that which you are promised﴾ refers to Paradise and Hell. Ibn Sirin said: ﴿And that which you are promised﴾ refers to the matter of the Hour. Al-Rabi' also said so.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So by the Lord of heaven and earth, indeed it is the truth.﴾ He emphasised what He had told them about the resurrection and about the provision He had placed in the sky, and He swore an oath by it that it is the truth. Then He reinforced it with His saying: ﴿just as it is that you speak﴾. He singled out speech from among the other senses, because the other senses may be subject to misperception: like what one sees in a mirror, the inability to taste when yellow bile dominates and the like, and the buzzing and ringing in the ear; whereas speech is free from all of that. Echo is not an objection to this, because it occurs only after speech has been produced by the speaker without being mixed with what could confuse it. Some of the wise said: just as every person speaks with his own self and cannot speak with the tongue of another, so every person eats his own provision and cannot eat the provision of another. Al-Hasan said: It has reached me that the Prophet ﷺ said: "May Allah fight against peoples to whom their Lord swore by Himself, and yet they did not believe Him." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So by the Lord of heaven and earth, indeed it is the truth.﴾ Al-Asma'i said: One day I came from the mosque of Basra when a rough, coarse Bedouin appeared, riding a she-camel, with his sword slung on him and his bow in his hand. He approached, greeted, and said: "From which people are you?" I said: "From the Banu Asma'." He said: "Are you al-Asma'i?" I said: "Yes." He said: "From where have you come?" I said: "From a place where the speech of the Most Merciful is recited." He said: "Does the Most Merciful have speech that humans recite?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then recite some of it to me." So I recited ﴿By those that scatter with dispersal (*al-Dhariyat dharwan*)﴾ until His saying: ﴿And in heaven is your provision﴾. He said: "O Asma'i, that is enough!" Then he went to his she-camel, slaughtered her, cut her up with her hide, and said: "Help me distribute her." We distributed her among those who came and went. Then he took his sword and bow, broke them, placed them under the saddle, and turned toward the desert, saying: ﴿And in heaven is your provision and that which you are promised﴾. I despised myself and blamed it. Then I performed the pilgrimage with al-Rashid. While I was circumambulating the House, I suddenly heard a soft voice. I turned, and there was the Bedouin, emaciated and yellowish. He greeted me, took my hands, and said: "Recite to me the speech of the Most Merciful." He seated me behind the Maqam, and I recited ﴿al-Dhariyat﴾ until I reached His saying: ﴿And in heaven is your provision and that which you are promised﴾. The Bedouin said: "We have found what the Most Merciful promised us to be true." Then he said: "Is there anything other than this?" I said: "Yes, Allah the Blessed and Exalted says: ﴿So by the Lord of heaven and earth, indeed it is the truth, just as it is that you speak﴾." The Bedouin gave a cry and said: "Glory be to Allah! Who has angered the Majestic, so that He swore an oath? Did they not believe Him in His word, until they forced Him to the oath?" He said it three times, and his soul departed with it. Yazid ibn Martad said: A man went hungry in a place where there was nothing, and he said: "O Allah, Your provision that You promised me, bring it to me." He was satisfied and quenched without food or drink. It is reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "If any of you were to flee from his provision, it would follow him just as death follows him." Al-Tha'labi transmitted it with its chain. In Sunan Ibn Majah it is reported from Habbah and Sawa', the two sons of Khalid, who said: "We entered upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was dealing with something, so we helped him with it. Then he said: 'Do not despair of provision as long as your heads move, for a human is born by his mother red, with no covering upon him (*qishr*, here meaning clothing), then Allah provides for him.'" It is also reported that a group of Bedouins sowed a crop, and a calamity struck it, so they grieved over it. A Bedouin woman came out to them and said: "What is wrong with you, that I see you have bowed your heads and your chests have become constricted? He is our Lord and the One who knows us; our provision is with Him, and He brings it to us wherever He wills!" Then she recited:

*Even if in a rock in the sea, firm,*
*solid, smooth on all sides,*
*there were a provision for a soul which Allah created,*
*it would split open until it delivered to it all that is within it.*

*Or if its path were between the layers of the seven heavens,*
*Allah would make easy for it the ascent to its rungs.*

*Until it attains what was written for it on the Tablet;*
*if it does not reach it, then it will come to it.*

I say: In this meaning is the story of the Ash'aris, when they sent their messenger to the Prophet ﷺ. He heard the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾, so he returned without speaking to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "The Ash'aris are not more insignificant to Allah than the beasts." We have already mentioned it in surah Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 6]]. Luqman said: ﴿O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed and be within a rock...﴾ the verse. This has passed in Luqman [[See vol. 14, p. 66]]. We have fully covered this topic in the book *Qam' al-Hirs bi-l-Zuhd wa-l-Qana'ah* (Suppressing Greed through Asceticism and Contentment), and praise belongs to Allah. This is true trust in God (*tawakkul*), which is not mixed with anything, and it is the emptiness of the heart with the Lord. May Allah grant us it, and not leave us dependent upon anyone other than Him, by His grace and generosity.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿just as it is that you speak﴾. The common reading (*qira'at al-'amma*) is *mithla* with a fatha, meaning "like" (*ka-mithl*) "*ma annakum*," so it is in the accusative by implicit omission of the *kaf*, meaning "like your speech," and *ma* is superfluous; this was said by some of the Kufans. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: it may be in the accusative as an emphasis, meaning "it is truly a truth like your speech," as if it were an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. Sibawayh's view is that it is indeclinable, built because it was attached to a non-declinable element, and *ma* is superfluous for emphasis. Al-Mazini said: *mithl* with *ma* is like one word, so it was built on the fatha for that reason. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this, and said: some Arabs make *mithl* always accusative, so one says: "A man like you said to me" and "I passed by a man like you," with *mithl* in the accusative meaning "like." Abu Bakr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-A'mash read *mithlu* with a damma, as an adjective of *haqqun*, because it is indefinite even though it is attached to a definite noun, since it is not restricted by attachment due to the multitude of things after which similarity occurs between similar things. *Mithl* is attached to *annakum*, and *ma* is superfluous, and it does not together with what follows act as a verbal noun, since there is no verb with it of which it could be a verbal noun. It is also permissible that it be a substitute for *haqqun*.

Awn ibn Abi Shaddad narrated that Jibril touched the calf with his wing, and it got up, running, until it reached its mother, and the mother of the calf was in the house. The meaning of (knowing) is that after he reached maturity he would be among those possessing knowledge of God and His religion. The majority hold that the one given good news of was Isaac. Mujahid alone said it was Ishmael, but this is nothing, for God, Exalted is He, says: (And We gave him good news of Isaac) [[see vol. 15, p. 99]]. And this is a clear text.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verses 29–30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then his wife came forward in a *sarrah*﴾, meaning in a cry and an outcry, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. From this comes the *sarir* of the door (the creaking), which is its sound. 'Ikrimah and Qatadah said: it is the wailing and the moaning. This "coming forward" was not a movement from one place to another. Al-Farra' said: it is like your saying, "He came forward to insult me," meaning he began to insult me. It was also said: she came forward *in a sarrah*, meaning in a group of women, hearing the speech of the angels.

Al-Jawhari said: the *sarrah* is the outcry and the shout; the *sarrah* is also the group; and the *sarrah* is the intensity of distress or other things. Imru' al-Qays said:

*So he overtook him with the leaders (of the wild cattle), and behind him their stragglers, in a sarrah that did not disperse.* [[Another reading is "fa-alhaqanā" (so he overtook us). The verse is from his mu'allaqah. The "hadiyat" are the first of the wild cows, and "jawahiruha" are their laggards. "Lam tazayyal" means did not scatter. He says: when this horse overtook the first of the wild cows, the last of them remained, not scattered.]]

This line admits of all three meanings. And the *sarrat al-qayz* is the intensity of its heat. When Sarah heard the glad tidings, she *sakkat wajhaha*, that is, she struck her hand upon her face, in the manner of women when they are astonished, as Sufyan al-Thawri and others said. Ibn 'Abbas said: she slapped her face. The origin of *sakk* is striking; *sakkahu* means he struck him. The rajiz (poet) said: [[He is Mudrik ibn Hisn. The full line is: "Then he sprinkled (him) with dung, and when he sprinkled..."]]

*O wild partridge, he struck you, so you crouched.*

Al-Umawi said: *kaban al-zabyu* means the gazelle lay flat on the ground when it pressed itself, and *iktabana* means it contracted.

(And she said, "An old barren woman.") That is, how would an old barren woman bear a child? Al-Zajjaj said: meaning she said, "I am an old barren woman, so how shall I bear?" just as she said: ﴿Woe is me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman?﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 69.]]

(They said, "So it is.") That is, as we said to you and informed you, (said your Lord), so do not doubt it. There was a year between the glad tidings and the birth. Sarah had not given birth before that, and she bore a child when she was ninety-nine years old, and Abraham was then a hundred years old. This has already passed.

(Indeed He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.) Wise in what He does, knowing of the interests of His creation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verse 31–37:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was certain that they were angels, by the bringing of the calf and the good tidings, he said to them: "What is your business" (fa-ma khatbukum), i.e., what is your matter and your story, "O messengers" (ayyuha al-mursalun).

﴿They said, "We have been sent to a guilty people"﴾ meaning the people of Lut.

﴿To send down upon them stones of clay﴾ i.e., to stone them with them.

﴿Marked﴾ (musawwamah), i.e., distinguished. It was said: they were striped with black and white. It was said: with black and red. It was said: (musawwamah) means known as stones of punishment. It was said: upon each stone was the name of the one who would be destroyed by it. It was said: upon them were the likenesses of seals. All of this has already passed in (Hud) [1]. So the stones would pursue their travelers and stragglers, and none of them escaped to bring news.

﴿With your Lord﴾ i.e., with Allah, and He had prepared them for stoning whoever was decreed to be stoned. Then it was said: they were baked like bricks; this was said by Ibn Zayd, and it is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿stones of sijjil﴾, as its explanation has already passed in (Hud). It was also said: they are the stones we see, whose origin is clay, and they become stones through the sun's burning of them over the passing of ages. He said "of clay" only so that it would be known that they are not hailstones, which are called stones of water. This was related by al-Qushayri.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers﴾ i.e., when We intended to destroy the people of Lut, We brought out those among his people who were believers, so that the believers would not perish. This is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So travel with your family﴾ [1].

﴿We found in it none but one house of the Muslims﴾ meaning Lut and his two daughters, and there is an ellipsis in it, i.e., "We found in it none but one household." It may be said "a noble house," meaning the family. His saying "in it" refers to the town, though no mention of it has preceded, because the meaning is understood. Also, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have been sent to a guilty people﴾ indicates the town, since a people only dwell in a town. It was said: the pronoun in "in it" refers to the group. "Believers" and "Muslims" here are the same, so the wording was varied to avoid repetition, as He said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah﴾ [see vol. 9 pp. 82, 79 and 215]. It was also said: faith (iman) is the assent of the heart, and Islam is submission outwardly; so every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer. Thus He called them "believers" in the first verse, because there is no believer who is not a Muslim. This meaning has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [vol. 1 p. 193] and elsewhere. His saying: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We believe." Say, "You have not believed"﴾ indicates the distinction between iman and Islam, which is the implication of the hadith of Jibril (peace be upon him) in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere. We have explained this in more than one place.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We left in it a sign﴾ i.e., a lesson and a mark for the people of that time and those after them; its parallel is: ﴿And We have certainly left of it a clear sign for a people who reason﴾ [vol. 13 p. 343]. Then it was said: the sign left behind is the ruined town itself. It was said: the piled stones with which they were stoned are the sign.

﴿For those who fear﴾ because they are the ones who benefit [in one manuscript: "those who are apprehensive"].

[1] See the earlier references in the commentary on Surah Hud.

﴿We found in it none but one house of the Muslims﴾ meaning Lut and his two daughters, and there is an ellipsis in it, i.e., "We found in it none but one household." It may be said "a noble house," meaning the family. His saying "in it" refers to the town, though no mention of it has preceded, because the meaning is understood. Also, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have been sent to a guilty people﴾ indicates the town, since a people only dwell in a town. It was said: the pronoun in "in it" refers to the group. "Believers" and "Muslims" here are the same, so the wording was varied to avoid repetition, as He said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah﴾ [see vol. 9 pp. 82, 79 and 215]. It was also said: faith (iman) is the assent of the heart, and Islam is submission outwardly; so every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer. Thus He called them "believers" in the first verse, because there is no believer who is not a Muslim. This meaning has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [vol. 1 p. 193] and elsewhere. Say, "You have not believed"﴾ indicates the distinction between iman and Islam, which is the implication of the hadith of Jibril (peace be upon him) in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere. We have explained this in more than one place.

Then it was said: the sign left behind is the ruined town itself. It was said: the piled stones with which they were stoned are the sign.

﴿For those who fear﴾ because they are the ones who benefit [in one manuscript: "those who are apprehensive"].

﴿They said, "We have been sent to a guilty people"﴾ meaning the people of Lut.

﴿To send down upon them stones of clay﴾ i.e., to stone them with them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verses 38–40:

Allah's words: ﴿And in Musa (Moses)﴾, meaning: We also left a sign in the story of Musa. Al-Farra' said: it is coordinated with His words, "And in the earth are signs" (﴿وَفِي الْأَرْضِ آيَاتٌ﴾), so that it reads "and in Musa."

(﴿When We sent him to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) with a clear authority﴾), meaning with a clear proof, which was the staff. It was also said: meaning with the miracles, including the staff and other things.

Allah's words: ﴿So he turned away with his pillar﴾, meaning Fir'awn turned away from faith. (*With his pillar*), meaning with his host and his troops, as said by Ibn Zayd. This is also the meaning given by Mujahid, and from it comes His saying, "or I could take refuge in a strong pillar" (﴿أَوْ آوِي إِلَى رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾), meaning protection and kinsfolk. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: with his strength. From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

*"The rigours of war have not weakened my pillar,
but rather what has passed of my time."* [In another narration: "nor has time's hand reached it."]

It was also said: with himself. Al-Akhfash said: with his side, as in His saying, "He turned away and withdrew his side" (﴿أَعْرَضَ وَنَأَى بِجَانِبِهِ﴾). This was also said by al-Mu'arrij. Al-Jawhari said: the *rukn* (pillar) of a thing is its strongest side, and "he takes refuge in a strong pillar" means in might and protection. Al-Qushayri said: the *rukn* is the side of the body. This is an expression of extreme turning away from a thing.

(﴿And they said: a sorcerer or a madman﴾). Here *aw* (أَوْ, "or") is in the sense of *wa* (وَاوٌ, "and"), because they said both of them together. This was said by al-Mu'arrij and al-Farra', who cited the verse of Jarir:

*"Do you equal the Tha'labah of the horsemen, or Riyah,
and make them equal to Tuhayyah and al-Khashshab?"* [Tuhayyah, on the pattern of Sumayyah, is a tribe of Tamim named after their mother; al-Khashshab are also clans of Tamim.]

*Aw* may be used in the sense of *wa*, as in His saying, "And do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one" (﴿وَلَا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِمًا أَوْ كَفُورًا﴾). And *wa* may be used in the sense of *aw*, as in His saying, "Then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four" (﴿فَانْكِحُوا مَا طَابَ لَكُمْ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ مَثْنَى وَثُلَاثَ وَرُبَاعَ﴾). All of this has been mentioned before.

(﴿So We seized him and his troops﴾) because of their disbelief and their turning away from faith.

(﴿And We cast them into the sea﴾), meaning We threw them into the sea.

(﴿while he was blameworthy﴾), meaning Fir'awn, because he committed what deserved blame.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verse 41–42:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And in ʿAd﴾, meaning: and We left in ʿAd a sign for whoever reflects.

(When We sent upon them the barren wind) — and it is the one that does not fertilize clouds or trees, and there is no mercy in it, no blessing, and no benefit. From this comes the expression "a barren woman," who does not conceive or give birth. Then it was said: it is the south wind (al-Janub). Ibn Abi Dhi'b narrated from al-Harith ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The barren wind is the south wind." Muqatil said: it is the west wind (al-Dabur), as in the Sahih from the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was helped by the east wind (al-Saba), and ʿAd was destroyed by the west wind (al-Dabur)." Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is al-Nakba' (a wind blowing between two directions). ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: its dwelling is the fourth earth, and what was opened upon ʿAd of it was no more than the size of a bull's nostril. Ibn Abi Najih also narrated from Mujahid that it is al-Saba (the east wind). And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It leaves nothing it comes upon without making it like that which is crumbled﴾, meaning like crushed, brittle matter. It is said of vegetation when it dries and crumbles: ramim and hashim. Ibn ʿAbbas said: like a perished, decayed thing, and Mujahid said the same. From this is the saying of the poet [[It is Jarir, lamenting his son.]]:

You left me when time took away my sight,
and I remained like the decayed bone of a rimma.

Qatadah said: it is that which has been trodden from dry vegetation. Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Suddi said: like pulverized dust. Qutrub said: al-Ramim is ash. Yaman said: what cattle have cast out of fodder by their chewing. It is said of the lip: al-mirammah and al-miqammah (with kasra), and al-marammah (with fatha) is a dialectal variant of it. The root of the word is from ramma al-ʿazm, when it decays. You say of it: ramma al-ʿazm yarimmu (with kasra) rimmah, so it is ramim. The poet said:

And he saw the consequences of breaking that as blame,
remaining upon him while the bones are ramim.

Al-rimmah (with kasra) means decayed bones, and its plural is rimam and rimam. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿It destroys everything﴾, as has preceded.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verses 43–45:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And in Thamud﴾, meaning: in them too there is a lesson and a sign, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a while in this world" (﴿until a time﴾), meaning until the time of destruction, which was three days, as in Hud: [[See vol. 9, p. 60.]] ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾. It is also said that the meaning of "enjoy yourselves" is: submit and enjoy yourselves until the end of your appointed terms.

(﴿So they defied the command of their Lord﴾), meaning they opposed the command of God, so they hamstrung the she-camel. (﴿Then the thunderbolt seized them﴾), meaning death. It is also said that it is every destroying punishment. Al-Husayn ibn Waqid said: every "thunderbolt" (sa'iqah) in the Qur'an is punishment. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid and al-Kisa'i read (al-Su'qah). It is said: "The man was struck (su'iqa) with a stroke (sa'qah) and a swooning (tas'aqan)," meaning he fainted. And "the sky struck them" (ṣa'aqat-hum al-samaʾ), meaning it cast the thunderbolt upon them. [[In manuscripts H, Z, L, N: "when it cast."]] The thunderbolt is also a cry of punishment, and it has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 219.]] and elsewhere.

(﴿While they were looking on﴾), at it, by day.

(﴿So they were not able to rise up﴾). It was said: the meaning is they could not stand up. It was also said: they were unable to bear God's punishment, to endure it, to stand up to it, and to repel it from themselves. You say, "I cannot stand up to this matter," meaning I cannot bear it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: meaning their bodies perished while their spirits remained in the punishment.

(﴿Nor were they able to defend themselves﴾), meaning they were unable to ward off the punishment when they were destroyed; that is, they had no helper.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: meaning their bodies perished while their spirits remained in the punishment.

(﴿Nor were they able to defend themselves﴾), meaning they were unable to ward off the punishment when they were destroyed; that is, they had no helper.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verse 46:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the people of Noah before﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i (a Kufan reader of the Qur'an) and Abu 'Amr read *wa-qawmi Nuhin* (وَقَوْمِ نُوحٍ) with *al-khafd* (the genitive case, *jarr*), meaning: "And in the people of Noah there is also a sign." The rest read it with *al-nasb* (the accusative case), meaning: "And We destroyed the people of Noah." It may also be coordinated with the *ha'* and *mim* (the pronoun suffixes) in *fa-akhadhathumu* (فَأَخَذَتْهُمُ), meaning: "So the thunderbolt seized them, and it seized the people of Noah." Or it is coordinated with the *ha'* in *akhadhnahu* (أَخَذْنَاهُ), or with the *ha'* and *mim* in *fa-nabadhnahum fi al-yamm* (فَنَبَذْنَاهُمْ فِي الْيَمِّ), meaning: "And We cast the people of Noah [into the sea]."

Or it may be in the sense of *udhkur* (اذكر), "remember."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verse 47–49:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the heaven We constructed with might﴾. When He had explained these verses, He said: "And in the heaven are signs and lessons that indicate the Creator is capable of perfection." So He joined the matter of the heaven to the story of the people of Noah, because both are signs. The meaning of (bi-ayd) is: with strength and power. From Ibn Abbas and others.

(And indeed, We are expanding it) Ibn Abbas said: "Capable." It was said: meaning, indeed We are of vast capacity, and with its creation and the creation of other than it, nothing We wish is constrained for Us. It was said: meaning, indeed We are expanding provision for Our creation. Also from Ibn Abbas. Al-Hasan said: "And indeed We are able." Also from him: "And indeed We are expanding provision by the rain." Al-Dahhak said: "We have made you rich," its evidence being: ﴿upon the affluent according to his means﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 203]]. Al-Qutabi said: "Possessing vastness over Our creation." The meanings are close. It was also said: We placed between them and the earth a vastness. Al-Jawhari said: "Awsa'a al-rajul" means the man became possessed of abundance and wealth, and from this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the heaven We constructed with might and indeed We are expanding it﴾, meaning: rich and capable. Thus it encompasses all the sayings.

(And the earth – We spread it out) meaning: We spread it out like a bed upon the surface of the water and stretched it.

(So how excellent are the spreaders!) meaning: how excellent are We as the Spreaders for them [[The word (lahum) is omitted from z.]]. The meaning of the plural here is glorification. "Mahadtu al-firash mahdan": I spread the bed, spreading it out and making it smooth. "Tamhid al-umur" means arranging and setting them right.

His saying, the Exalted: (And of everything We created pairs) meaning: two kinds and two different types. Ibn Zayd said: meaning male and female, sweet and sour, and the like. Mujahid said: meaning male and female, the heaven and the earth, the sun and the moon, the night and the day, the light and the darkness, the plain and the mountain, the jinn and the humans, the good and the evil, the morning and the evening, and like the differing things of tastes, scents and sounds; that is, We made this like that as a proof of Our power, and whoever is able to do this is able to restore. It was also said: (And of everything We created pairs) so that you may know that the Creator of pairs is singular, so no motion or stillness, no light or darkness, no sitting or standing, no beginning or end, may be ascribed to His attributes, since He, Mighty and Majestic, is One (Witr) [[See vol. 16, p. 8]] "there is nothing like unto Him." (So that you may remember.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 51, verse 50–55:

(His saying, may He be exalted:) ﴿So flee to Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾ When the account had preceded of how their nations denied their prophets and were destroyed, Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet ﷺ: "Say to them, O Muhammad." That is, say to your people: ﴿So flee to Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾ That is, flee from His disobedience to His obedience. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Flee to Allah by repenting from your sins." And from him: "Flee from Him to Him, and act in obedience to Him." Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: ﴿So flee to Allah﴾: "Go out to Makkah." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "Guard yourselves against everything other than Allah, for whoever flees to other than Him will not be protected from Him." Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "Flee from obedience to Satan to obedience to the Most Merciful." Al-Junayd said: "Satan is a caller to falsehood, so flee to Allah, who will protect you from him." Dhu al-Nun al-Misri said: "Flee from ignorance to knowledge, and from disbelief to gratitude." 'Amr ibn 'Uthman said: "Flee from your selves to your Lord." He also said: "Flee to what has preceded for you from Allah, and do not rely on your own movements." Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: "Flee from what is other than Allah to Allah."

(﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner.﴾) That is, I warn you of His punishment for disbelief and disobedience. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not set up with Allah another god.﴾ He commanded Muhammad ﷺ to say this to the people, and he is the warner. It was also said: it is an address from Allah to the creation.

(﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him﴾) That is, from Muhammad and his swords (﴿a warner﴾), that is, I warn you of his might and his sword if you associate others with Me. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus there came not to those before them any messenger except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ This is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ: just as your people denied you and said, "Sorcerer" or "Madman," those before them denied and said the like of their saying. The kaf in ﴿thus﴾ may be in the accusative, under the assumption "I warn you with a warning like the warning of those messengers who came before me and warned their peoples," or in the nominative, under the assumption "the matter is thus," that is, like the first. The first is a frightening of those among the monotheists who disobey Him, and the second is for those among the atheists who associate others with Him. The pause on His saying ﴿thus﴾ is reported from Ya'qub and others.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did they charge one another with this?﴾ That is, the first of them enjoined on the last of them the denial, and they conspired upon it. The alif is for rebuke and wonder.

(﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾) That is, they did not enjoin on one another; rather, transgression gathered them, and transgression is exceeding the limit in disbelief.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them and pardon them. (﴿So you are not blameworthy﴾) before Allah, because you have discharged what was upon you of conveying the message. Then this was abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers.﴾ It was also said: it was abrogated by the verse of the sword. The first is the saying of al-Dahhak, because he was commanded to face them with admonition. Mujahid said: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them; ﴿so you are not blameworthy﴾, that is, your Lord does not blame you for any shortcoming on your part; ﴿and remind﴾, that is, with admonition, for admonition ﴿benefits the believers.﴾ Qatadah said: ﴿And remind﴾ with the Qur'an, ﴿for the reminder﴾ by it ﴿benefits the believers.﴾ It was also said: remind them with punishment and the days of Allah. He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from it.
